items.explain: Q27: The question asks for **earlier examples** of blindfold chess. The passage says *'displays of the feat go back centuries'* and mentions a game in *'13th-century Florence'*. So the answer is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: In 1947, the Argentinian grandmaster Miguel Najdorf played 45 simultaneous games in his mind, winning 39 in the 24-hour session.
Accomplished players can develop the skill of playing blind even without realising it.
The nature of the game is to run through possible moves in the mind to see how they play out.
From this, regular players develop a memory for the patterns the pieces make, the defences and attacks.
"You recreate it in your mind," said Gareyev.
"A lot of players are capable of doing what I'm doing."
The real mental challenge comes from playing multiple games at once in the head.

Not only must the positions of each piece on every board be memorised, they must be recalled faithfully when needed, updated with each player's moves, and then reliably stored again, so the brain can move on to the next board.
items.explain: Q28: The question asks what blindfold chess **involves**. The passage explains you must *'memorise'* positions, *'recall'* them, *'update'* them with moves, and *'store'* them again. This outlines the process, so the answer is **E**.

items.sentence_raw: First moves can be tough to remember because they are fairly uninteresting.
But the ends of games are taxing too, as exhaustion sets in.
items.explain: Q32: The question asks why the **last part** of a game is difficult. The passage directly says *'the ends of games are taxing too, as exhaustion sets in'*. **'Taxing'** means difficult, and **'exhaustion'** is the reason, so the answer is **E**.

items.sentence_raw: When Gareyev is tired, his recall can get patchy.
He sometimes makes moves based on only a fragmented memory of the pieces' positions.
The scientists first had Gareyev perform some standard memory tests.
items.explain: Q37: The passage says *'The scientists first had Gareyev perform some standard memory tests'*. The researchers tested his **memory**, so the answer is **'memory'**.

items.sentence_raw: These assessed his ability to hold numbers, pictures and words in mind.
One classic test measures how many numbers a person can repeat, both forwards and backwards, soon after hearing them.
items.explain: Q38: The passage describes a test: *'how many numbers a person can repeat, both forwards and backwards'*. He had to recall a string of **numbers**, so the answer is **'numbers'**.

items.sentence_raw: Most people manage about seven.
"He was not exceptional on any of these standard tests," said Rissman.
"We didn't find anything other than playing chess that he seems to be supremely gifted at."
items.explain: Q29: The question says Gareyev's skill is **limited to chess**. The passage quotes a researcher: *'We didn't find anything other than playing chess that he seems to be supremely gifted at'*. This means his special talent is only in chess, so the answer is **F**.

items.sentence_raw: But next came the brain scans.
With Gareyev lying down in the machine, Rissman looked at how well connected the various regions of the chess player's brain were.

Though the results are tentative and as yet unpublished, the scans found much greater than average communication between parts of Gareyev's brain that make up what is called the frontoparietal control network.
items.explain: Q39: The scans found *'much greater than average communication between parts of Gareyev's brain'* in the network that directs attention. So there was unusual **communication**, and the answer is **'communication'**.

items.sentence_raw: Of 63 people scanned alongside the chess player, only one or two scored more highly on the measure.
"You use this network in almost any complex task.
It helps you to allocate attention, keep rules in mind, and work out whether you should be responding or not," said Rissman.
It was not the only hint of something special in Gareyev's brain.
The scans also suggest that Gareyev's visual network is more highly connected to other brain parts than usual.
items.explain: Q40: The scans suggested his *'visual network is more highly connected'*, meaning the parts dealing with **visual** input might be stronger. So the answer is **'visual'**.

items.sentence_raw: Initial results suggest that the areas of his brain that process visual images - such as chess boards - may have stronger links to other brain regions, and so be more powerful than normal.
While the analyses are not finalised yet, they may hold the first clues to Gareyev's extraordinary ability.
For the world record attempt, Gareyev hopes to play 47 blindfold games at once in about 16 hours.
He will need to win 80% to claim the title.
"I don't worry too much about the winning percentage, that's never been an issue for me," he said.
